extracted.intended_audience: general public, legal practitioners, and researchers interested in patent litigation (especially design-patent damages)
extracted.subtask_description: Summary of legal standards and practical litigation criteria arising from Apple Inc. v. Samsung Electronics Co., focusing on what counts as the relevant 'article of manufacture' for design-patent damages and related procedural and evidentiary issues in patent disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article of manufacture (design-patent damages)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'article of manufacture,' as used in Patent Act provision governing damages for design patent infringement, encompasses both a product sold to a consumer and a component of that product, and components of the infringing smartphones could be the relevant 'article of manufacture,' although consumers could not purchase those components separately from the smartphones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court reversed the lower-court damages award and remanded to the Federal Circuit to define the appropriate legal standard for what qualifies as the relevant 'article of manufacture' — i.e., courts must decide whether damages should be measured by the entire product sold to consumers or by a component/part to which the design pertains. This determination directly affects the scope of recoverable profits/damages for design-patent infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages purpose — compensatory not punitive
rubrics_metrics.description: "The damages award should put the patent holder in approximately the financial position it would have been in had the infringement not occurred" and "it is meant to compensate the patent holder and not to punish an infringer."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court instructions and legal principle require damages to compensate for lost position, not to punish. Jury comments that an award should be "sufficiently high to be painful" contradict this rule and can prompt scrutiny or appellate review of the award amount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornamental-design requirement for design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Design-patent claims at issue were one-sentence claims about the ornamental design of an electronic device, accompanied by figures (e.g., a thin rectangular cuboid with rounded corners). Design patents therefore protect the ornamental (non-functional) appearance of an article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting a design patent, the focus is on ornamentation as shown in drawings; infringement and scope analyses look to the ornamental features rather than functional aspects. The particular drawings and what they disclose (including broken lines, figures) are central to claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility-patent functional-claim coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility patents at issue covered functional features such as the iPhone's 'bounce-back effect', 'on-screen navigation', and 'tap to zoom' functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility patents protect functional and technical innovations; infringement findings for utility patents depend on claim construction and comparison to accused products' functionality. Functional patents are subject to validity challenges (e.g., by PTO reexamination) and prior-art attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent invalidity based on prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Some patents at issue were declared invalid based on existing prior art (e.g., Federal Circuit panel ruled patents invalid based on prior art; USPTO tentatively invalidated certain patents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art can invalidate asserted patents post-trial (through appeals or USPTO proceedings), which may nullify jury awards. Patent challengers may seek reexamination/IPR or raise prior-art defenses at trial; validity challenges can substantially change remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement as factor in verdicts
rubrics_metrics.description: The jury found that Samsung had willfully infringed on Apple's design and utility patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finding of willfulness may affect the magnitude of damages and the court's discretion regarding injunctive relief; willfulness findings often lead to requests for enhanced damages or other sanctions, but they are subject to legal standards and appellate review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunction and irreparable-harm standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Apple filed motions to stop sales of accused Samsung products; one motion was denied by Judge Koh because Apple's claims of irreparable harm had little merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To obtain a preliminary (or permanent) injunction, a patentee typically must show irreparable harm, likelihood of success on the merits, balance of equities, and public interest. Denial of an injunction can be reviewed on appeal and may be reversed if a higher court finds the irreparable-harm showing sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade dress and dilution claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The jury found that Samsung had diluted Apple's trade dress related to the iPhone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade dress (distinctive non-functional product appearance or packaging) can be asserted alongside patents; dilution or trade-dress infringement findings may yield damages or injunctions but are evaluated under trademark/trade-dress law distinct from patent law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence integrity and admissibility (no tampering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apple submitted side-by-side image comparisons that were later found to have been tampered with to make features seem more similar, and Samsung accused Apple of submitting misleading evidence to the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authenticity and reliability of evidence are critical; tampered or misleading exhibits can undermine credibility, lead to sanctions, evidentiary exclusion, or reversal of rulings. Parties must ensure documentary and demonstrative evidence is accurate and not misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury competence and complexity of instructions in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions were raised about the validity of lay juries in complex patent cases — qualifications of jury members were deemed inadequate, and the jury received more than 700 questions yet reached a quick verdict; there were subsequent allegations of juror misconduct and undue reliance on a juror's technical expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex patent cases place heavy demands on jury comprehension and quality of instructions; courts must balance the right to jury trial with the need for clear instructions, appropriate voir dire, and sensitivity to juror expertise or misconduct. Flaws in jury process can be grounds for retrial or appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic and scope considerations for injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts issued and rescinded injunctions with varying geographic scope (e.g., an EU-wide injunction later rescinded and limited to German market; different national courts reached inconsistent results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope of injunctive relief may be limited geographically or by product; national courts may differ in remedies and scope, and enforcement can be affected by multi-jurisdictional litigation, appeals, and evidence issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-trial adjustments and appellate review of remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: The district court and subsequent proceedings adjusted damages repeatedly (jury awarded $1.049 billion; district court reduced to $290 million; later adjustments and appeals resulted in other amounts such as $539 million), and higher courts vacated or reinstated parts of awards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages and remedies in high-stakes patent litigation are frequently modified on post-trial motions, judicial recalculation, and appeal. Parties should expect potential changes to awards during appeals, remands, and related proceedings (including PTO actions).
